---
title: "Animation"
description: >
  Non-reactive keyframe animation: compile a plot into one keyframe per state,
  train the scales once over every state and freeze them, then tween and encode
  the in-between frames (GIF, APNG or animated SVG) in vellum's parallel Rust
  backend.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = requireNamespace("vellumplot", quietly = TRUE)
)
library(vellumplot)

# Show one frame of an animation in the page: anim_frame() to a temporary PNG,
# inlined as a data URI.
show_frame <- function(animation, frame = NULL, alt = "") {
  f <- anim_frame(tempfile(fileext = ".png"), animation, frame = frame, scale = 2)
  knitr::asis_output(sprintf(
    '<img src="%s" alt="%s" style="width:100%%;max-width:576px">',
    knitr::image_uri(f),
    alt
  ))
}
```

An animated plot is a sequence of still plots played in quick succession. In
vellumplot the stills are **keyframes** — one compiled plot per *state* — and the
frames between them are **tweened**: their marks are interpolated so a point
glides from where it sits in one state to where it sits in the next.

This is *non-reactive* keyframe animation. The states are decided up front (the
levels of a column), and the scales are trained **once over every state and then
frozen**. Nothing retrains between frames: the axis breaks, the colour ramp and
the size legend are the same in every frame, so the eye can read motion against a
fixed backdrop. Animation is not a live/reactive runtime — it is a fixed set of
states compiled ahead of time.

## The pipeline

Four verbs, added to any plot:

* `transition_states(states)` — marks the column whose levels are the states.
* `ease_aes(ease)` — chooses the easing (how the interpolation accelerates).
* `animate(nframes, fps)` — compiles the keyframes and returns a
  `vellum_animation`.
* `anim_save(file, animation)` — tweens and encodes the frames to a file.

```{r}
#| eval: false
library(gapminder)

vplot(gapminder) |>
  mark_point(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") |>
  transition_states(year, transition_length = 2, state_length = 1) |>
  ease_aes("cubic-in-out") |>
  animate(nframes = 100, fps = 25) |>
  (\(a) anim_save("gapminder.gif", a))()
```

The output format follows the file extension: `.gif` for a looping animated GIF
(universally viewable), `.png` or `.apng` for an animated PNG (APNG — lossless,
with transparency), or `.svg` for an animated SVG. The tween, the parallel render
across CPU cores, and the streaming encode all happen in one pass in vellum's
Rust backend.

### Animated SVG, and choosing a format

`.svg` writes a single **animated SVG**: every frame is emitted as vector markup
and shown in turn by a CSS step animation. Two things make it worth reaching for.
It is **resolution-independent** — the same file is crisp in a slide, on a retina
screen, and in print, which no raster format is. And it honours
**`prefers-reduced-motion`**: a reader who has asked their system not to animate is
shown one still frame, with no extra work from you -- the last frame when the
animation ends on its final state (a reveal, `transition_time()`, a non-looping
`transition_states()`), otherwise the first. Each animated SVG namespaces its CSS,
so several can share one HTML page.

The trade-off is size. Because every frame is emitted in full, an animated SVG
grows with the number of marks times the number of frames, where a GIF does not.
So it wins clearly on **line art** — a handful of moving marks, the common
explanatory case — and loses on a **dense scatter**, where a raster format is the
right answer. Choose by mark count, not by preference; `anim_save()` says so when
a `.svg` scene is dense enough that a raster format would likely be smaller. Serve
it gzipped (`.svgz`, or a web server with compression) to shrink it several-fold.

```r
p |> animate() |> (\(a) anim_save("draw.svg", a))()
```

### Video and WebP

There is no video or animated WebP encoder among vellum's dependencies, so
`anim_save()` does not write `.mp4`, `.webm` or `.webp`. Given one of those
names it stops and tells you what to do instead: save an APNG or a GIF and
convert it.

```sh
ffmpeg -i anim.png -pix_fmt yuv420p anim.mp4
```

```r
magick::image_write(magick::image_read("anim.gif"), "anim.webp")
```

## A bar chart race

The viral "bar chart race" needs no special API — it is an ordinary
`transition_states()` animation over long-format data. Because each bar is keyed
by its category, the tween slides bars past one another as their ranks change
between states, and the frozen scales keep the value axis from jumping.

```r
set.seed(1)
cats <- c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E")
race <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2000:2006, function(y)
  data.frame(year = y, cat = cats,
             value = pmax(1, runif(5, 1, 10) + (y - 2000) * c(2.5, 1, 0.4, 3, 1.6)))))

vplot(race) |>
  mark_bar(x = cat, y = value, fill = cat) |>
  coord_flip() |>
  transition_states(year, transition_length = 2, state_length = 1) |>
  labs(title = "Bar chart race") |>
  animate(nframes = 60, fps = 12) |>
  (\(a) anim_save("race.gif", a))()
```

`coord_flip()` makes the bars horizontal (the familiar racing layout); rank the
categories within each year first if you want them sorted top-to-bottom.

## What a keyframe looks like

`animate()` compiles one keyframe per state. `anim_frame()` saves any single
frame as a still PNG, SVG or PDF; here is the first frame of an
`mtcars`-by-cylinder animation, the first state. Each car is its own mark,
keyed by `data_id` (see [Which mark becomes which](#which-mark-becomes-which)):

```{r}
cars <- transform(mtcars, car = rownames(mtcars))

a <- vplot(cars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, size = hp, color = factor(cyl), data_id = car) |>
  transition_states(cyl) |>
  ease_aes("cubic-in-out") |>
  animate(nframes = 60, fps = 20)
```

```{r}
#| eval: false
anim_frame("keyframe.png", a, frame = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_frame(a, 1, alt = "A scatter of weight against miles per gallon showing only the four-cylinder cars, on axes that cover every car.")
```

The keyframes themselves are ordinary vellum scenes, in `a@scenes` (one per
state), so you can also inspect one with vellum's tools.

## Posters and stills

`anim_frame(filename, animation, frame)` is the way to get a poster, a
thumbnail, or the moment to put in print. The frame is drawn exactly as it
appears in the animation, with the same frozen scales, tween and frame
variables, so the poster matches the animation it stands for. A static plot
built separately from one state would train its scales on that state alone.

Frames are numbered as in the saved file, pauses and rewind included (see
[Timing](#timing)). Leave `frame` out to get the frame a reader who asks for
reduced motion sees: the final frame when the animation ends on its last state,
otherwise the first.

```{r}
#| eval: false
anim_frame("poster.png", a)              # the reduced-motion frame
anim_frame("middle.svg", a, frame = 25)  # a mid-transition frame, as vector
```

## Frozen scales — the non-reactive guardrail

Because the scales are trained once over the pooled states, the domain is the
*union* across every state. A point that is extreme in one state and typical in
another keeps a stable position reference throughout: the axes never jump. This is
the observable proof that the animation stayed non-reactive — compare the axis
breaks of any two keyframes and they are identical, even though the two states'
data cover very different ranges.

Per-state *statistics* still recompute (a smooth is refit per state, a bin count
re-tallied), but no scale *domain* retrains. Retraining a scale in response to the
data of the moment would be a reactive runtime, which vellumplot is deliberately
not.

## Easing

`ease_aes()` shapes how the interpolation fraction moves through each transition.
`"linear"` is a constant rate; a family name with a direction suffix eases in, out,
or both:

* families: `quad`, `cubic`, `quart`, `quint`, `sine`, `expo`, `circ`, `back`,
  `elastic`, `bounce`
* directions: `-in`, `-out`, `-in-out`

`"cubic-in-out"` — slow start, quick middle, slow finish — reads as the most
natural motion for most plots.

The easing can differ per aesthetic. `ease` sets the default, and `position`,
`color` (or `colour`), `size` and `alpha` each override it for one class of
property:

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Bars settle into place gently while the fill crossfades at a steady rate.
ease_aes("cubic-in-out", color = "linear")
```

`position` covers x and y together (and every other coordinate, such as bar
widths and path vertices); it also decides when discrete attributes switch.
`alpha` covers the fade of marks entering and leaving.

## What tweens, and what does not

Between two keyframes, an element's **position**, **size**, **alpha**, and
**colour** interpolate — colour perceptually, in Oklab, so a hue transition stays
vivid instead of passing through grey. Discrete attributes (a marker shape, a line
type, a text label) do not interpolate continuously; they snap at the midpoint.

### Which mark becomes which

Marks tween by **identity**, as gganimate matches by group. A mark of one state
moves into the mark that is the same thing in the next state, however the rows
are ordered. A mark's identity is:

1. its `data_id`, when the layer has one (`mark_point(..., data_id = country)`);
2. otherwise its group: the `group` aesthetic if mapped, else the combination
   of the layer's discrete mapped aesthetics (`color`, `fill`, `shape`, a
   discrete `x`, and so on), so a bar race's bars keep their colours as they
   slide between ranks;
3. and within a group, the order of its rows.

A line, path or area is one mark per series and is matched by its group.

Row order is the last resort. It is enough when each group has one mark per
state, but when a group has several rows and changes size between states, rows
pair up by position and a point may jump to another row's place. `animate()`
tells you once when that can happen and suggests a `data_id`; give the layer one
(or a `group`) when its rows are individual observations.

### Entering, leaving and morphing

A mark found in only one of two adjacent states **enters** (fades in) or
**exits** (fades out) on the alpha easing: points, bars, tiles, labels, lines
and areas alike. A point whose colour group changes slides to its new place
while its colour blends. A line, path or area whose number of points changes
**morphs** from one outline into the other.

What cannot move switches whole halfway through the transition: decoration
without an identity that comes and goes, or a line that cannot be morphed (a
line broken by missing values, say). `animate()` warns once when that will
happen and names the states.

Give each transition enough frames to be seen: `nframes` is spread over all
the states, so 40 states in 80 frames leave two frames per state and nothing
visibly moves.

### Missing values

Rows with a missing position or size draw nothing, as in a static plot, and
`animate()` says so once per layer for the whole animation ("Removed n rows
containing missing values"). The count includes rows that are in no frame at
all, such as those with a missing state.

## Faceted animations

A faceted plot animates panel by panel. Every panel of the whole data is drawn
in every frame: a state with no rows for a panel leaves that panel empty rather
than changing the layout. A mark's identity includes its panel, so a mark never
slides from one panel into another. A row whose facet value changes between
states fades out of one panel and into the other.

```{r}
af <- vplot(cars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(gear), data_id = car) |>
  facet_wrap(~am, labeller = label_both) |>
  transition_states(cyl) |>
  animate(nframes = 30, fps = 10)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_frame(af, 8, alt = "Two facet panels, am 0 and am 1, part-way from the four- to the six-cylinder state: the four-cylinder cars fade out as the six-cylinder cars fade in.")
```

The scales are frozen across frames, so per-panel scales can't be honoured:
`facet_wrap(scales = "free")` (or `"free_x"`, `"free_y"`) and an independent
`resolve_scale()` on a position stop `animate()` with an error that says to use
fixed scales. `transition_reveal()` works with facets too.

## Frame variables

Titles can count along with the animation. A title, subtitle or caption set
with `labs()` may embed frame variables in braces, glue-style, as in gganimate.
Each `{...}` is an R expression evaluated for every frame, not only at the
keyframes, so a `{frame_time}` title counts through the in-between times while
the marks move. Write `{{` and `}}` for literal braces.

* every transition: `frame`, `nframes`, `progress` (`frame / nframes`);
* `transition_states()`: `closest_state`, `previous_state`, `next_state` and
  `transitioning` (`TRUE` while moving);
* `transition_time()`: `frame_time`, the time the frame has reached;
* `transition_reveal()`: `frame_along`, the `along` value revealed so far.

```{r}
#| eval: false
vplot(gapminder) |>
  mark_point(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") |>
  transition_time(year) |>
  labs(title = "Year: {round(frame_time)}") |>
  animate(nframes = 100, fps = 25)
```

A `mark_text()` label can use the same variables. The label is placed (and
moves) like any mark, and only its string changes per frame, so a large year
behind a bubble chart is one more layer:

```{r}
#| eval: false
mark_text(
  data = data.frame(x = 3000, y = 40), x = x, y = y,
  label = "{round(frame_time)}", size = 60, color = "grey85"
)
```

Repelled and rich-text labels are not templated. An ordinary data label whose
string differs between two states takes the nearer state's string, switching
halfway through.

## Continuous time

`transition_time()` is the continuous-time sibling of `transition_states()`: it
treats the column as a time and allocates frames **in proportion to each time
gap**, so the animation runs at a constant rate even when the times are unevenly
spaced. Time flows once — no pause on a state, no wrap.

```{r}
#| eval: false
vplot(gapminder) |>
  mark_point(x = gdpPercap, y = lifeExp, size = pop, color = continent) |>
  scale_x_continuous(trans = "log10") |>
  transition_time(year) |>
  animate(nframes = 100, fps = 25) |>
  (\(a) anim_save("gapminder.gif", a))()
```

The time may be numeric, `Date` or `POSIXct`. Dates and date-times are spaced
by their day or second gaps, and `{frame_time}` keeps their class (and time
zone), so `labs(title = "{format(frame_time, '%d %b %Y')}")` works.

## Reveal

`transition_reveal(along)` is a different kind of animation: instead of tweening
between states, it **reveals the data along `along`**, as gganimate does — the
classic "line draws itself". Each frame shows the rows whose `along` value has
been reached. Points appear as they are reached; a line, path, area, ribbon or
step grows through its rows with an interpolated leading point, each series
toward its own next row. The scales are frozen over the whole data, and the
background, grid, axes and legends are drawn whole throughout.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
walk <- data.frame(t = 1:60, y = cumsum(rnorm(60)))

ar <- vplot(walk) |>
  mark_line(x = t, y = y) |>
  mark_point(x = t, y = y) |>
  transition_reveal(t) |>
  labs(title = "t = {round(frame_along)}") |>
  animate(nframes = 30, fps = 10)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
show_frame(ar, 15, alt = "A random walk drawn up to about t = 30 of 60, on axes that already cover the whole series.")
```

`along` may be numeric, `Date` or `POSIXct`, and needn't be the x axis: a
spiral revealed by angle, or a `coord_flip()` series, unrolls in data order.
Each frame is its own keyframe, so `animate()` compiles `nframes` scenes.

## Timing

`transition_length` and `state_length` are *relative* durations: how long the
moving segments last versus the held pauses on each state. `nframes` is the total
frame count and `fps` the playback rate, so the animation runs for `nframes / fps`
seconds. `wrap = TRUE` (the default) loops the last state back to the first.

`animate()` also takes gganimate's `start_pause`, `end_pause` and `rewind`.
The pauses hold the first and last frame for that many frames, and
`rewind = TRUE` plays the animation back to the start so the loop doesn't cut.
They come out of `nframes`: `animate(nframes = 100, end_pause = 20)` moves for
80 frames and rests on the final picture for 20. Every output follows them:
`anim_save()` to GIF, APNG or SVG, the frame numbers of `anim_frame()`, and the
frame scrubber of an animated vellumwidget.

```{r}
#| eval: false
p |>
  transition_states(year, wrap = FALSE) |>
  animate(nframes = 100, fps = 25, end_pause = 25) # hold the end for a second
```
